items.title: Decoding Graded Grip‐Force Intensity From fMRI Data Reveals a Transformation From Abstract to Effector‐ and Movement‐Specific Codes Prior to Execution
items.author: Guido Caccialupi,  Timo Torsten Schmidt,  Felix Blankenburg
items.content:
In an fMRI study, we used a delayed grip-force task and time-resolved MVPA to examine where in the brain graded force intensities are parametrically represented, whether they are encoded in an abstract, effector-independent format, and how these representations are subsequently transformed into effector- and movement-specific codes. During the first delay period (Delay 1), above-chance decoding was observed in the precuneus/superior parietal lobule (PCu/SPL), whereas during the second delay period (Delay 2), it appeared in effector-specific regions, including the contralateral intraparietal sulcus (pIPS/aIPS) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd). These findings indicate a transformation from abstract representations of force intensity in the PCu/SPL to effector- and movement-specific plans in the aIPS and PMd, as further corroborated by cross-effector decoding and cross-temporal generalization.

Motor planning entails a progressive transformation of neural representations - from abstract motor goals, which represent intended action-outcomes independent of any particular effector (i.e., the body part executing the action), to effector-specific movement plans. Functional MRI (fMRI) studies have shown that parametric variations in parietal activity patterns reflect the encoding of intended force-intensities in effector-specific regions, even before detailed movement parameters are specified. However, how these intended force-intensities are initially represented in an abstract, effector-independent format and subsequently transformed into effector- and movement-specific plans remains unclear. To address this, human-participants performed a delayed grip-force task during fMRI. They first prepared two of four possible force-intensities, then received a cue indicating which hand should apply which force, and finally executed both grips simultaneously. Using time-resolved support vector regression (SVR) combined with a searchlight approach, we identified brain-regions that parametrically code grip-force intensities across two 6-s delay periods. During the first delay, above-chance decoding was observed in a medial section of the posterior parietal cortex spanning the precuneus and superior parietal lobule (PCu/SPL), whereas during the second delay it emerged in effector-specific regions, including the contralateral intraparietal sulcus (pIPS/aIPS), primary somatosensory cortex (S1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and supplementary motor area (SMA). Cross-decoding confirmed effector-independent coding in the PCu/SPL, while cross-temporal generalization revealed stable representations in the contralateral IPS and PMd from the second delay through execution. Together, these findings indicate a progressive transformation from abstract representations of intended force-intensity in the PCu/SPL to effector- and movement-specific plans in the IPS and PMd.

items.title: Multimodal Brain Graph Analysis for Uncovering Path‐Based Biomarkers in Schizophrenia: Integrating Static and Dynamic Approaches
items.author: Haleh Falakshahi,  Hooman Rokham,  Daniel H. Mathalon,  Judith M. Ford,  Bryon A. Mueller,  Adrian Preda,  Theo G. M. van Erp,  Jessica A. Turner,  Godfrey Pearlson,  Vince D. Calhoun
items.content:
A multimodal framework integrating time-resolved fMRI connectivity and gray matter features enables estimation of static and dynamic brain graphs. Path-based analysis identifies disrupted connectors and disconnectors in schizophrenia, revealing network alterations undetectable by unimodal or pairwise approaches and highlighting potential biomarkers of disease.

Analyzing multimodal brain networks offers new insights into the mechanisms of brain disorders. However, most studies focus on unimodal networks or use global/local graph metrics, often missing critical information about disrupted pathways. In this study, we propose a novel framework for estimating static and dynamic multimodal brain graphs by integrating time-resolved functional network connectivity (FNC) and gray matter features using a Gaussian graphical model. We then apply a path-based graph theory analysis to identify connectors and disconnectors, edges that respectively introduce or eliminate paths in the patient graph compared to controls. Our findings in schizophrenia reveal several edges linked to missing or additional paths, indicating network disruptions that are undetectable using unimodal or pairwise analyses. These disrupted pathways span both within- and cross-modal connections, particularly involving regions like the middle temporal gyrus and cerebellum. This work demonstrates the value of multimodal integration and emphasizes the importance of moving beyond individual edge-level analysis when characterizing disease-related network alterations. Our path-centric approach provides a complementary view of brain connectivity disruption and identifies candidate path-based markers of schizophrenia that warrant validation in independent datasets.

items.title: Major Depressive Disorder With Non‐Suicidal Self‐Injury in Adolescents: Altered Morphological Inverse Divergence Gradient in Brain Structure and Gene Expression Patterns
items.author: Yan Zhang,  Xinyuan Hu,  Wei Wang,  Jing Wang,  Hongying Li,  Yumei Wan,  Jianlei Zhu,  Fei Liu,  Shiyue Tao,  Duanwei Wang,  Xiangtao Lin,  Yingying Zhang,  Hongmei Zhang,  Yuandong Gong
items.content:
Using the morphometric inverse divergence gradient network (MIND-Gd), this study shows that adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD) and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) exhibit altered principal structural gradients relative to adolescents with MDD without NSSI, and that these gradient changes are spatially coupled to neurotransmitter receptor distributions and to the expression of synaptic and neurodevelopmental genes across cortical layers and cell types.

Adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD) and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) face serious challenges to their mental and physical health. The development of this condition is influenced by genetic, environmental, and brain development factors. In this study, we used the Morphometric Inverse Divergence Gradient Network (MIND-Gd) for the first time to explore brain structural network abnormalities and their transcriptional mechanisms in adolescents with MDD and NSSI. A total of 241 adolescents with MDD participated in this study. Among them, 134 had NSSI, while 107 did not. Using high-resolution T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we constructed the principal MIND gradient network. This network reflects the similarity of cortical morphology between different brain regions. The results showed that adolescents with NSSI had higher MIND gradient values in the left caudal middle frontal gyrus and bilateral inferior temporal gyri. In contrast, lower values were observed in the left lingual gyrus and right superior parietal lobule. These structural changes were spatially correlated with functional alterations in the dorsal attention network. Further analysis revealed that these differences were linked to the distribution of nine types of neurotransmitter receptors, including 5-HT1A, GABAa, glutamate, and dopamine. Partial least squares regression analysis (PLS) was also conducted. The first component (PLS1) explained 39.53% of the spatial variance in MIND-Gd. This analysis identified key genes related to NSSI, such as GABRA5 and MGST1. Enrichment analysis showed that PLS1+ genes were involved in synaptic signaling, neurodevelopment, and mood disorder pathways. These genes were enriched in astrocytes and cortical layers I, II, and V. On the other hand, PLS1− genes were linked to chromatin regulation and cytoskeletal metabolism. These genes were mainly expressed in Cortical Layers III and IV. In conclusion, adolescents with MDD and NSSI show specific abnormalities in brain structural gradients. These abnormalities are closely related to neurotransmitter receptor distributions and gene expression patterns. The findings provide multi-level evidence for understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of NSSI.

items.content:
From large multi-site lifespan data, we segment C1–C7 and derive morphometric measures (area, diameters, shape). Normative centile charts summarize population trajectories across age and sex and provide a practical scoring framework to quantify where an individual lies relative to expected variation.

Spinal cord morphometry provides essential biomarkers of neurological health, but clinical interpretations are confounded by inter-subject variability and a lack of normative references across the full human lifespan. We address this gap by generating the first comprehensive lifespan charts for cervical spinal cord morphometry. From 78,269 T1-weighted brain MRI sessions, we identified a final cross-sectional cohort of 24,251 healthy or cognitively normal controls from 33 datasets (ages 0–100 years) with cervical cord coverage. To overcome contrast variability, we employed a state-of-the-art contrast-agnostic deep learning segmentation method, extracting cross-sectional area (CSA), anteroposterior (AP) and right–left (RL/transverse), and shape indices (AP/RL ratio, eccentricity, and solidity) from C1 to C7. Normative trajectories were modeled using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS). The resulting charts reveal distinct non-linear lifespan changes: rapid growth through childhood and adolescence, peak maturation occurring in early-to-mid adulthood (e.g., mid-30s for CSA), followed by gradual decreases. Significant regional variations along the cervical cord and consistent sex differences (males > females for size metrics) were quantified. Spinal cord trajectories showed strong temporal coupling with brain white matter and brainstem volumes, suggesting integrated CNS development and aging. These lifespan charts provide a robust normative framework, enabling age- and sex-specific centile scoring of individual spinal cord morphometry. This resource offers a critical tool for differentiating typical variation from pathological changes, enhancing the clinical utility of spinal cord MRI in studies of development and neurodegeneration.

items.title: Inside a Programmer's Brain: Dissociating Code and Language Comprehension Networks Using a Novel fMRI‐ESM Protocol
items.author: Victor Cepero‐Escribano,  Patricia León‐Cabrera,  Anna Gasa‐Roqué,  Xavier Otazu,  Alejandro Fernandez‐Coello,  Pablo Naval‐Baudin,  Àngels Camins,  Immaculada Rico,  Andreu Gabarros,  Antoni Rodriguez‐Fornells,  Xim Cerda‐Company
items.content:
Personalized intraoperative mapping using programming tasks enabled the identification and preservation of code-related eloquent cortex, supporting postoperative recovery of professional programming abilities.

Code comprehension and natural language share structural similarities but engage partially distinct neural systems. While language predominantly recruits the classical perisylvian language network, code comprehension has been linked to the multiple-demand system, associated with mathematical thinking and problem solving. We report the case of a professional software engineer with an IDH-mutant astrocytoma in the left middle frontal gyrus, a region where these networks converge. To address the potential risk of impairing computer programming abilities during surgery, we implemented a personalized protocol combining fMRI and intraoperative electrical stimulation mapping (ESM), extending the standard language assessment with a task. Intraoperative mapping identified sites in the left inferior frontal cortex that were functionally relevant to the task but were not identified during standard object-naming mapping. Complete tumor resection was achieved while preserving these critical regions, with the patient showing intact post-operative language and programming performances. This single case study suggests that individualized mapping may identify functionally relevant sites not detected by standard object-naming mapping, supporting the potential clinical value of tailored fMRI–ESM protocols for preserving higher-order cognitive functions in neurosurgical patients.

items.title: Functional Imaging of Hippocampal Layers Using VASO and BOLD on the Next Generation (NexGen) 7T Scanner
items.author: Suvi Häkkinen,  Alexander Beckett,  Erica Walker,  Laurentius Huber,  David A. Feinberg
items.content:
CBV VASO based fMRI was optimized on NexGen 7T for layer-specific hippocampal imaging and tested using an autobiographical memory task. Depth dependent activation profiles based on VASO and BOLD images from the same acquisition differed particularly in subiculum, consistent with activation mislocalization in BOLD profiles due to venous bias.

Spatial accuracy and venous biases are a central concern in mesoscale fMRI, with subcortical brain regions facing additional challenges due to lower sensitivity, high physiological noise, and complicated vasculature. Here, we optimized CBV VASO on the NexGen 7T scanner for layer-specific investigations of the human hippocampus. Both VASO and BOLD (from the same acquisition) detected significant hippocampal activation during an established autobiographical memory task. At the macroscale, activation patterns converged, showing pronounced memory task activation in the anterior hippocampus and consistent engagement across the frontoparietal neocortex. At the laminar scale, however, differences in depth-dependent profiles emerged within the subiculum: BOLD exhibited a pronounced bias toward the inner layers, consistent with the known venous drainage pattern in the subfield. Finally, the optimized effective TR of 3.2 s allowed exploratory study of retrieval stages and neocortical functional connectivity, which both supported hippocampal anterior–posterior dissociation using either VASO or BOLD. Thus, hippocampal fMRI allows mapping layer function with high accuracy and can provide deeper insights into a number of neuropsychological phenomena and disorders.
